title: Twenty years of praising India is not a China strategy
gist: Two decades of Western diplomatic embrace of India never became a capital pivot: China's inward FDI stock lead over India has widened from hundreds of billions to more than US$3 trillion, and India's 2025 FDI inflows were only about 37% of China's. The author argues the West is mistakenly demanding alignment from India when what it needs is scale, and that only state action changing the conditions for private capital — not corporate 'China plus one' decisions — can build an industrial counterweight.

themes.theme: The political pivot without the capital pivot

insights.claim: Western governments have called India indispensable to the 21st-century order for 20 years, dating to George W. Bush's 2005 break with American orthodoxy, but treated the breakthrough as diplomatic realignment rather than the start of an industrial rebalancing.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Twenty years of rhetoric with no capital flow means India-exposure narratives should be tested against FDI data, not summit communiqués.
insights.quote: The political pivot occurred. The capital pivot did not.
insights.locator: For 20 years, Western governments have described India

insights.claim: When Bush struck the civil nuclear bargain in 2005, China's stock of inward foreign direct investment was already roughly seven times India's, and China's absolute lead has since expanded from hundreds of billions of dollars to more than US$3 trillion.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: The FDI stock gap widened despite two decades of pro-India rhetoric — the base case for supply-chain diversification timelines should be measured in decades, not cycles.
insights.quote: India’s stock has risen, but China’s absolute lead has expanded from hundreds of billions of dollars to more than US$3 trillion.
insights.locator: When Bush struck the civil nuclear bargain

insights.claim: In 2025 India's FDI inflows were only about 37% of China's, meaning that even if India eventually overtook China on new inflows, closing the inherited stock gap could take decades.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Hard constraint on the 'India replaces China' trade: flow-based optimism ignores stock-based inertia — position for a multi-decade, not multi-year, rebalance.
insights.quote: In 2025, India’s FDI inflows were only about 37% of China’s

themes.theme: Cumulative industrial advantage as a self-reinforcing loop

insights.claim: Industrial advantage compounds endogenously: each new factory in China strengthened logistics, deepened supplier networks and expanded technical capability, so the conditions that attracted capital were increasingly the product of capital already invested.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: A reflexivity model for manufacturing clusters — it implies relocation costs rise over time and that late movers need subsidy to overcome, not merely match, incumbent economics.
insights.quote: The conditions that attracted capital were increasingly the product of capital already invested.

insights.claim: Western commercial optimisation over three decades, accelerating after China's 2001 WTO entry, ended up aligning with Beijing's own strategy of reducing exposure to foreign technology while preserving China's centrality to global manufacturing, producing asymmetric dependence.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: The dependence is one-directional by design; expect Chinese export-control and chokepoint leverage to keep being used because the asymmetry is structural, not incidental.
insights.quote: What served Western commercial optimisation has come to align with Chinese strategy.

insights.claim: China retains the ports, suppliers, components, skills and industrial density that rising industrial powers are still trying to build, so firms nominally pursuing 'China plus one' still face incentives that favour staying in China.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Treat corporate 'China plus one' announcements skeptically — the unit economics still point back to China absent policy change.
insights.quote: China has the ports, suppliers, components, skills and industrial density that rising industrial powers are still trying to build.
insights.locator: The West is trying to correct a compounded strategic error

themes.theme: Policy error: outsourcing rebalancing to firms

insights.claim: The core policy failure is mistaking the accumulation of fragmented corporate decisions for strategic rebalancing, with governments asking individual firms to bear the cost of reversing a concentration created by decades of collective investment and reinforced by Western policy.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Implies de-risking policy as currently designed will underdeliver — watch for a shift toward state-backed industrial finance as the tell that this critique has landed.
insights.quote: The policy failure is to mistake the accumulation of fragmented corporate decisions for strategic rebalancing.
insights.locator: The policy failure is to mistake

insights.claim: Building a genuine industrial alternative requires governments to alter the conditions under which private investment becomes commercially rational at scale, rather than directing individual investments.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: A test for any de-risking program: does it change the hurdle rate economy-wide, or just subsidise a handful of named projects?
insights.quote: Building a genuine alternative requires governments to alter the conditions under which private investment becomes commercially rational at scale, not to direct individual investments.

insights.claim: Vietnam, Mexico and Indonesia can absorb specific industries and create valuable redundancy, but none can anchor a self-reinforcing industrial alternative at continental scale — only India can.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Differentiates the friendshoring trade: Vietnam/Mexico are cyclical beneficiaries; India is the only structural systemic alternative.
insights.quote: Vietnam, Mexico, Indonesia and others can absorb specific industries and create valuable redundancy. But none can anchor a self-reinforcing industrial alternative at continental scale.

insights.claim: India does not need to absorb every industry currently concentrated in China or replicate China's industrial model, but no alternative supply network can acquire comparable strategic weight without India at its centre.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Frames India as the network hub rather than a one-for-one substitute — value accrues to India's connective infrastructure, logistics and component base.
insights.quote: But no alternative network can acquire comparable strategic weight without India at its centre.
insights.locator: India need not absorb every industry

insights.claim: India's uneven infrastructure, administrative complexity, skills base and manufacturing depth are arguments for structuring investment and reform intelligently, not for pretending another country offers comparable scale.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: The bear case on India is real but non-substitutable — the practical question is execution design, not country selection.
insights.quote: Those are reasons to structure investment and reform intelligently, not to pretend another country offers comparable scale.

insights.claim: Modi has spent more than a decade trying to convert India's demographic and geopolitical scale into industrial power with promising but uneven results, and India cannot become a second centre of industrial gravity through domestic reform alone.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: India's manufacturing story is gated on foreign capital inflows, not just Delhi's reform agenda — track FDI, not just PLI schemes.
insights.quote: But India cannot become a second centre of industrial gravity through domestic reform alone.
insights.locator: Modi has spent more than a decade

themes.theme: Strategic autonomy is a feature, not a defect

insights.claim: Treating India as a participant inside a US-and-allies-designed architecture is a category error: unlike middle powers such as Australia and Canada that exercise influence through alliances and coalition-building, India is an independent strategic pole.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: A classification error with policy consequences — expect recurring Western frustration and repeated mispricing of India's willingness to follow Washington.
insights.quote: Western policy often treats India as a participant within an architecture designed by the United States and its allies. That is a category error.

insights.claim: India is the world's most populous country, a nuclear-armed continental state, an Indian Ocean power and an economy projected to become the world's third largest by the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: The third-largest-economy milestone by 2030 is the anchor date for long-horizon India allocation decisions.
insights.quote: the world’s most populous country, a nuclear-armed continental state, an Indian Ocean power and an economy projected to become the world’s third largest by the end of the decade
insights.locator: India is an independent strategic pole

insights.claim: India will bargain, hedge, dissent and pursue its own interests rather than follow Washington on Russia or subordinate other relationships, but the same strategic autonomy that frustrates Washington also constrains Beijing.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: India will not be coerced into sanctions alignment — discount headlines predicting a decisive India tilt in either direction.
insights.quote: The strategic autonomy that frustrates Washington also constrains Beijing.
insights.locator: It will not. India will bargain

insights.claim: The West is demanding greater alignment from the country it needs to strengthen than it ever demanded from the adversary it allowed itself to depend upon — a failure to distinguish control from advantage.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: The central asymmetry in Western Indo-Pacific policy; resolving it in India's favour would unlock a much larger capital reallocation than current programs imply.
insights.quote: That is not prudence. It is a failure to distinguish control from advantage.
insights.locator: The West is demanding greater alignment

insights.claim: The strategic objective should not be an aligned India but an India large enough to make dependence on China optional, since alignment is desirable while scale is indispensable.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Reframes the metric of success in Indo-Pacific policy from votes at the UN to installed industrial capacity in India.
insights.quote: The strategic objective is not an aligned India. It is an India large enough to make dependence on China optional.
insights.locator: The strategic objective is not an aligned India

insights.claim: India is Australia's fifth-largest export market and 11th-largest import source but ranks only 21st as a destination for Australian investment, exposing a trade-versus-capital gap in the relationship.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: A quantified gap that Australian policy is likely to target — watch Australian superannuation and critical-minerals capital flows toward India.
insights.quote: India is Australia’s fifth-largest export market and 11th-largest import source, but ranks only 21st as a destination for Australian investment.
insights.locator: Australia cannot finance India’s industrial transformation

insights.claim: Australia cannot finance India's industrial transformation but can integrate critical minerals, energy and defence cooperation into a broader industrial strategy, following a Modi–Albanese summit package spanning defence, maritime security, energy, critical minerals and resilient supply chains.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Campbell
insights.so_what: Critical minerals and defence-industrial cooperation are the concrete deal channels to monitor in the Australia-India relationship.
insights.quote: But it can integrate critical minerals, energy and defence cooperation into a broader industrial strategy.
insights.locator: Australia cannot finance India’s industrial transformation
